subject: History of USA
title: 21. Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances

segments.text: If a candidate can draw who checks whom and give one real constitutional example for each arrow, they understand this topic — and separation of powers (federal branches) must never be confused with federalism (national-state division, Topic 5).

blocks.text: How the Branches Check Each Other

segments.text: Congress can refuse funding, conduct investigations, override vetoes, reject nominations or treaties in the Senate, and impeach/remove federal officials through the House-Senate process. The president can veto legislation and use executive visibility and administrative authority to shape policy, with veto threats often influencing legislation before a bill even reaches the White House. Federal courts can hold laws or executive actions unconstitutional through

(Topic 5), though courts depend on cases being brought before them and cannot enforce every decision independently; presidents nominate federal judges and the Senate confirms them, giving the political branches real influence over judicial composition in turn.

Foreign affairs, appointments, budgeting and war powers all demonstrate that constitutional powers overlap by deliberate design, requiring cooperation rather than complete control by any single branch. When different parties control Congress and the presidency (
), institutional checks intensify — gridlock may frustrate policy, but it is also a direct product of a system deliberately designed to make large changes difficult without broad agreement.

items.text: The situation where different parties control Congress and the presidency, intensifying institutional checks and often producing legislative gridlock.

Create a triangle diagram: Congress checks president/courts; president checks Congress and appoints judges; courts review laws/executive actions; add real constitutional examples rather than memorising abstract definitions.
Do not define separation of powers as complete isolation of the branches; many powers are shared by design.
Do not confuse checks and balances with federalism.
Do not assume judicial review gives courts unlimited power; courts are constrained by jurisdiction, precedent, appointments and constitutional structure.
The president may veto legislation; Congress can override with a two-thirds vote in each chamber.
The Senate confirms many appointments and consents to treaties by required supermajority.
Marbury v. Madison (1803) is the foundational case establishing judicial review.
Separation of powers means controlled interaction and shared power by design, never complete isolation of the three branches.

Keep separation of powers (horizontal, among federal branches) and federalism (vertical, national-state) permanently distinct — the single most valuable precision point across both this topic and Topic 5.
